title: BoJ meets with rates at a 31-year high and the yen near 158
deck: The Bank of Japan is expected to hold at 1.25% on 30 October, but any hint of a move to 1.5% in December would test a weak yen, Japanese bond yields and foreign debt markets such as France's.

card.headline: The BoJ is expected to hold on 30 October; the signal about December is what matters

keyNumber.label: BoJ policy rate, the highest since April 1995, with USD/JPY near 158

forYou.line: A hold is the base case. Watch for guidance toward 1.5% as early as December, and for the new inflation forecasts published the same day.
A yen near 158 raises the cost of imported oil and food. It also flatters exporters' overseas earnings.

forYou.role: Anyone holding French or other foreign bonds
forYou.line: Higher Japanese yields can pull Japanese investors home. They are large holders of French OATs, so French borrowing costs are exposed.
A weak yen keeps Japan cheap for visitors. It keeps energy and food costs high for people living there.

effects.text: BoJ decision on 30 October: a hold at 1.25% is expected, with the guidance on further hikes the real news
The Quarterly Outlook Report lands the same day with updated growth and inflation forecasts
USD/JPY near 158 moves on tone: hawkish guidance can lift the yen, cautious guidance can push it weaker
Japanese government bond yields reprice to the guidance on the pace of tightening
A firmer yen can force carry-trade positions funded in yen to unwind, as happened in August 2024
Japanese importers face higher energy bills while the yen is weak and oil is elevated
Higher domestic yields give Japanese institutions a reason to hold more JGBs and fewer foreign bonds
A weak yen near 158 raises the chance of Ministry of Finance action
French and other euro-area bond buyers lose some of their Japanese demand just as France needs to raise record funds in 2027
The ECB (29 October) and the BoJ (30 October) face the same energy-driven inflation, so global yields can drift up together
Japan's interest bill on its large public debt rises as rates climb, narrowing fiscal room

whatHappened: The Bank of Japan holds its two-day policy meeting, ending on 30 October. The policy rate stands at 1.25%, the highest since April 1995.
The board raised rates on 18 September by a 7-2 vote. The gap between that hike and the one before it is the shortest since 1990, according to the event summary.

On 19 October, Governor Kazuo Ueda said underlying inflation is 'quite close' to the 2% target. He also flagged elevated crude oil as an upside risk to prices. The yen held steady near 158 per dollar after those remarks.

Markets expect a hold in October. They are watching for any guidance that points to 1.5% as early as December. The Quarterly Outlook Report, with the bank's updated forecasts, is published on the same day as the decision.
whyItMatters: Japan imports nearly all of its crude oil. The US-Israel war on Iran, which began on 28 February 2026, has kept oil and freight costs high. That feeds the same inflation risk the board flagged in September.
The yen sits near 158. A weak currency raises import costs and adds to inflation. That pushes the BoJ toward further hikes, and the central bank must balance that against growth.
Japan has been the world's cheap funding source for years. When Japanese rates rise, money borrowed in yen to buy higher-yielding assets abroad becomes less attractive, and some of it can flow home.

Japanese investors are among the largest foreign holders of French government bonds. Higher JGB yields can reduce that demand just as France's borrowing premium is near its widest since the euro-debt crisis.

winners.who: Japanese savers and holders of yen
winners.why: Higher rates and a firmer yen would raise returns and restore some purchasing power. This is a conditional gain, since the yen remains weak.
A yen near 158 flatters overseas earnings when converted back, so a hold with soft guidance helps them.
Yields at multi-decade highs mean better returns, and domestic institutions may buy more JGBs and fewer foreign bonds.

losers.why: A weak yen plus elevated crude raises fuel, food and input costs.
A hawkish surprise could lift the yen sharply and force a rush to close positions.

losers.who: Governments reliant on Japanese bond demand, notably France
losers.why: If Japanese investors repatriate funds, borrowing costs for OATs can rise further.
Higher rates raise the cost of servicing a very large public debt over time.

whatsNext: 23 October: Moody's reviews France's Aa3 negative rating; Japanese demand for French debt is one of the risks around it.
29 October: the ECB decides on rates, with euro-area inflation at 3.8% and policymakers weighing another rise.
30 October: the BoJ announces its decision and publishes the Quarterly Outlook Report.
December: the next BoJ meeting, the earliest point at which markets see a move to 1.5%.

predict.explanation: Our base case, at about 50%, is a hold with hawkish-leaning guidance. A hold with no new signal is next at about 30%. A surprise hike and a disorderly yen move are each around 10%. These are author judgements, not sourced forecasts.

timeline.detail: He flags elevated crude oil as an upside risk. USD/JPY holds near 158.

causes.name: Exit from ultra-low rates
causes.detail: The BoJ has been moving away from its long-running easy policy, taking the rate to 1.25%, the highest since 1995.

causes.name: Import dependence
causes.detail: Japan buys nearly all of its crude oil abroad, so energy shocks pass quickly into prices.

causes.name: Large public debt
causes.detail: Higher rates raise the cost of servicing Japan's government debt over time.

causes.name: The 18 September hike
causes.detail: A 7-2 vote raised the rate to 1.25%. The pace of tightening is now the live question.

causes.name: Inflation near target
causes.detail: Ueda says underlying inflation is 'quite close' to 2%, which supports further hikes.

causes.name: Gulf energy shock
causes.detail: War with Iran and attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure kept oil elevated and added to the inflation risk the board flagged.

causes.name: Weak yen near 158
causes.detail: A weak currency raises import costs and adds to the case for tightening.

causes.name: Global rate pressure
causes.detail: The ECB is also weighing another rate rise as euro-area inflation reaches 3.8%.

stakeholders.name: Kazuo Ueda
stakeholders.wants: Reach the 2% target sustainably without disrupting markets or growth
stakeholders.leverage: Guidance at the press conference and the Quarterly Outlook Report
stakeholders.likelyMove: Hold, keep the door open to more hikes, and stress data dependence on oil and wages

stakeholders.name: BoJ board members who voted against the September hike
stakeholders.wants: Presumably a slower pace of tightening, though the material does not give their reasons
stakeholders.leverage: Their votes signal how much consensus there is for a December move
stakeholders.likelyMove: A repeat of caution is possible; a change in dissent would be a signal

stakeholders.name: Japan's Ministry of Finance
stakeholders.wants: Avoid disorderly yen weakness without undermining the BoJ
stakeholders.leverage: Currency intervention, as in past episodes of sharp yen weakness
stakeholders.likelyMove: Verbal warnings first; action if the yen weakens quickly

stakeholders.name: Japanese institutional investors
stakeholders.role: Large holders of foreign bonds, including French OATs
stakeholders.wants: Better returns at home as JGB yields rise
stakeholders.leverage: Repatriation of savings can lift foreign yields

stakeholders.name: Carry-trade investors
stakeholders.role: Borrow in yen to buy higher-yielding assets
stakeholders.leverage: Rapid unwinding can move equity and bond markets
stakeholders.likelyMove: Reduce exposure if the yen rises quickly on hawkish guidance

stakeholders.name: US Federal Reserve
stakeholders.role: Counterpart whose policy sets the rate gap that drives USD/JPY
stakeholders.wants: Not covered in the source material
stakeholders.leverage: The US-Japan rate gap influences the yen
stakeholders.likelyMove: Not estimated here; check the Fed's own guidance

sectors.why: Higher policy rates typically widen lending margins. This is a general pattern, not a sourced estimate.
A weak yen lifts overseas earnings when converted back.
Elevated crude and a yen near 158 raise input costs.
Higher yields hurt existing holders but attract new buyers.
Japanese investors are large holders of OATs, and repatriation can raise funding costs.
A sharp yen rise can force liquidations.
A weak yen makes the country cheaper for foreign visitors.

dailyLife.effect: With the yen near 158 and crude elevated, prices of imported energy and food stay high for Japanese households.
Variable-rate borrowers feel higher policy rates over time. Exact pass-through depends on the lender.
Deposit rates tend to follow policy rates upward, but slowly.

dailyLife.item: Overseas travel and imports for Japanese consumers
dailyLife.effect: A weak yen makes holidays abroad and imported goods more expensive.
A weak yen makes hotels, food and goods cheaper for visitors paying in other currencies.

scenarios.name: Hawkish hold
scenarios.looksLike: The BoJ holds at 1.25%. Ueda signals that inflation is near target and that oil is an upside risk, leaving December open. The yen firms modestly.
signposts: Outlook Report raises the inflation forecast
Press conference stresses upside risks and a gradual path
scenarios.effectOnWorld: A December hike becomes the market's base case; JGB yields edge up and some Japanese money returns home.

scenarios.name: Neutral or cautious hold
scenarios.looksLike: The BoJ holds and gives little guidance, citing uncertainty from the energy shock and growth.
signposts: Outlook Report trims growth or leaves inflation unchanged
Ueda says it is too early to judge the effect of the last hike
scenarios.effectOnWorld: USD/JPY drifts weaker; the yen near or above 158 keeps import costs elevated.

scenarios.name: Surprise hike to 1.5%
scenarios.looksLike: The board raises rates again, against market expectations, citing oil and a weak yen.
signposts: Government comments supporting action on the yen
scenarios.effectOnWorld: The yen jumps; carry trades unwind; global equities wobble and foreign bond yields rise.

scenarios.name: Disorderly yen move
scenarios.looksLike: USD/JPY pushes through 160 after a cautious hold, or whipsaws sharply, prompting verbal or actual intervention from the Ministry of Finance.
signposts: Sharp one-day moves in the yen
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Volatility spreads to bond and equity markets; the BoJ is pressed toward a faster hike.

predictions.text: The BoJ holds its policy rate at 1.25% on 30 October (probability 0.85).
At least one BoJ board member dissents in the 30 October decision (probability 0.3).
The BoJ raises its policy rate to 1.5% at or before its December meeting (probability 0.45).
USD/JPY trades above 160 at some point before year-end (probability 0.3).
Japan's Ministry of Finance intervenes in the currency market before year-end (probability 0.15).

actions: Importers: review hedging for yen exposure and energy costs around the 30 October decision.
Exporters: avoid assuming a weak yen persists; test budgets at a stronger rate.
Treat the Quarterly Outlook Report as a check on the BoJ's own inflation forecast.
Watch whether guidance points to December; a clear signal tends to firm the yen and lift JGB yields.
Check the size of yen-funded positions, since a sharp yen rise can force liquidation.
If you hold French bonds, add Japanese repatriation to the list of risks beside the Moody's review on 23 October.
In Japan: expect imported energy and food to stay costly while the yen is weak and crude is elevated.
Variable-rate borrowers: budget for gradual rises as the BoJ continues to tighten.
Travellers: plan foreign currency purchases around yen volatility.
Coordinate messaging so the BoJ and the Ministry of Finance do not send conflicting yen signals.
Assess the cost of debt service in a world of higher JGB yields.
Treat the energy shock as the shared driver of inflation across Japan and the euro area.

analogues.event: BoJ hike and global market sell-off
analogues.whatFollowed: A rate hike and hawkish tone in July 2024 helped drive a sharp yen rise and a steep equity sell-off in early August as carry trades unwound.
Japan's Ministry of Finance bought yen after sharp weakness, including around 160 per dollar in 2024; the effect on the currency was often temporary.
The BoJ ended its negative rate policy and began a slow path of hikes, with the yen staying weak for long stretches.

watch.title: USD/JPY near 160

watch.title: Oil prices
